craft_claim: Defiant voice draws its spine from moral conviction rather than preference: moral mandates are authority- and peer-independent, predict counter-conformity, and carry an ought that ordinary attitude strength does not.

supporting_evidence.location: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 88(6):895-917, Studies 1-3
supporting_evidence.note: Attitudes held with strong moral conviction (moral mandates) are perceived as objectively true and universal, are relatively authority- and peer-independent, and after controlling for attitude strength uniquely predict preferring greater social and physical distance from attitudinally dissimilar others.

supporting_evidence.location: Analyses of Social Issues and Public Policy 2(1):35-41
supporting_evidence.note: Moral mandates have high action potential because they are oughts and shoulds; the authors review how they can lead people to disregard procedural safeguards as well as to prosocial action.
Across a nationally representative sample, stronger moral conviction predicted greater distrust in authorities to decide a contested issue, distinguishing moral conviction from religiosity.

counterevidence.note: The same moral absolutism that gives a defiant voice force also predicts reduced tolerance of dissent, so moral vocabulary carries a documented rigidity cost as well as a motivational gain.

scope: Moral and civic argument, manifestos, and testimony where the speaker claims a principle rather than a preference.
exceptions: When moral language is used instrumentally without an underlying principle, audiences and research both register it as posturing rather than conviction.
In contexts where the audience does not share the moral predicate, the ought reads as imposition and raises reactance.
